query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin aluminide coating to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will allow in situ formation of a protective alumina scale at high temperature, thereby improving oxygen resistance without compromising its room-temperature ductility or high‐temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with a single‐phase (likely BCC) microstructure that shows 8–16% tensile ductility at room temperature and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin, adherent aluminide coating (via a pack cementation or vapor deposition method) on the alloy’s surface.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure at approximately 1000 °C in an oxidizing (air) atmosphere for up to ~100 hours; mechanical tests conducted at similar strain rates (10^−4–10^−2 s^−1) as in the baseline evaluations.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an in situ, dense, and adherent Al2O3 (alumina) layer on the surface, which acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
generation.mechanism: The aluminide coating reacts with oxygen at high temperature to form a continuous protective alumina scale. This scale prevents rapid oxygen ingress and oxidation of the underlying alloy, thereby preserving its intrinsic mechanical properties while significantly enhancing its oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy will show substantially reduced oxidation (lower weight gain and thinner, more adherent oxide scales) at 1000 °C while retaining similar yield strength and ductility to the untreated cast alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy, which suffers from poor oxygen resistance (rapid oxidation) under similar high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected to hold for exposure durations up to around 100 hours at ~1000 °C; longer exposures or significantly higher temperatures may alter the coating integrity or induce microstructural changes in the substrate.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal coating thickness and processing parameters (e.g., precise aluminide composition, deposition temperature) need to be determined; effects on other properties (such as fatigue or long-term coating adherence) remain to be assessed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr specimens: one group with the applied aluminide coating and a control group without coating. Expose both groups to 1000 °C in air for 100 hours. Afterwards, perform oxidation testing (measuring weight gain and oxide scale characterization using SEM/EDS) and high-temperature tensile tests under identical strain-rate conditions to evaluate yield strength and ductility.
measurements: Weight gain per unit area (oxide scale thickness assessment)
Surface and cross-sectional SEM/EDS analysis of the oxide scale
High-temperature tensile properties (yield strength and ductility)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminide-coated specimens either do not exhibit improved oxidation resistance (i.e., show similar oxide scale formation or weight gain as the control group) or suffer a significant deterioration in mechanical performance (substantially reduced yield strength or ductility compared to baseline values), the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Oxygen solute strengthening is an effective strategy to harden alloys, yet, it often deteriorates the ductility. Ordered oxygen complexes (OOCs), a state between random interstitials and oxides, can simultaneously enhance strength and ductility in high-entropy alloys. However, whether this particular strengthening mechanism holds in other alloys and how these OOCs are tailored remain unclear. Herein, we demonstrate that OOCs can be obtained in bcc (body-centered-cubic) Ti-Zr-Nb medium-entropy alloys via adjusting the content of Nb and oxygen. Decreasing the phase stability enhances the degree of (Ti, Zr)-rich chemical short-range orderings, and then favors formation of OOCs after doping oxygen. Moreover, the number density of OOCs increases with oxygen contents in a given alloy, but adding excessive oxygen (>3.0 at.%) causes grain boundary segregation. Consequently, the tensile yield strength is enhanced by ~75% and ductility is substantially improved by ~164% with addition of 3.0 at.% O in the Ti-30Zr-14Nb MEA. In the alloys with a given amount of Nb from 14 to 30 at.%, the yield strength increases with the oxygen content (Fig. 1c), demonstrating strong interstitial strengthening. For the ductility wise, when the Nb content is below 26 at.%, it increases with the oxygen concentration (i.e., the ductility change ratio of the doped MEA to the un-doped counterpart is positive) and reaches its maximum in the sample with 3.0 at.% oxygen (Fig. 1d). It is interesting to note that the strongest ductilization effect of oxygen was realized in the alloy with 14 at.% Nb, i.e., with addition of 3 at.% oxygen, the ductility is increased by 164 %.
